study.title: Psalm 135 Praise to the LORD above all
study.overview: This psalm summons the servants of God to praise him for whom he is and for what he did in the history of his people. The text unites adoration, memory and contrast: the Lord is good, great, sovereign over creation and faithful in the redemption of Israel, while idols are lifeless human works. The psalm ends by calling the whole community of the covenant to bless the Lord, whose presence in Zion and Jerusalem seals the tone of joy and reverence.

outline.title: Initial Invitation to the Praise
outline.explanation: The servants of the LORD, especially those who serve in his house, are called to bless his name. The main motive is the goodness of God and the beauty of his name, worthy of song and continuous gratitude.

outline.title: The sovereign greatness of the LORD in creation
outline.explanation: The psalmist claims that God chose Israel for himself and is incomparable among all the gods. He rules everything that exists, from the heavens to the seas, and manifests his power also in the phenomena of nature.

outline.title: The God who judges enemies and cares for his people
outline.explanation: God's action at the outgoing of Egypt and in the defeat of kings shows his dominion over the nations. At the same time, the psalm confesses that the name of the LORD abides forever and that he judges his people with compassion.

outline.title: The Vanity of Idols and the Adoration of the Covenant Community
outline.explanation: The idols are described as lifeless objects, made by human hands. In contrast, Israel, Aaron, Levi, and all who fear the LORD are summoned to bless him, concluding with the exaltation of the God who dwells in Jerusalem.

study.context: The psalm presents a liturgy of praise focused on the community of worship. The notes indicate a link with the previous psalms and the pattern of exhortation addressed to the priests, Levites and all the people of the covenant. The setting is that of worship in the holy space of God, with Zion and Jerusalem as central references at the close. The text also recalls remarkable events in Israel's history, such as the departure of Egypt and the conquest of the land, to support praise.
study.theology: Theologically, the psalm unites doxology and confession: God is good, great, sovereign and worthy of praise because he reigns over creation and history. He is not a local force or an idol made, but the living LORD, who does all that pleases him. His election of Israel is not human merit, but an expression of peaceful grace. The psalm also shows that God's judgment on enemies and their compassion for the people are not opposites, but two faces of their faithfulness. In denouncing the uselessness of idols, the text reaffirms that trusting in them leads to the spiritual ruin itself. The closure in Jerusalem highlights the presence of God in the midst of his people and the proper response: blessing, reverence and community worship.

scholarViews.insight: The expressions Jacob and Israel encompass all the people of the covenant; the Lord chose him as his special possession among all the nations.
The psalmist presents God's greatness as a matter of reverent praise, and this rests on the personal conviction that the Lord is really incomparable.
The final blessing is linked to the restoration of the temple and the city, with God dwelling in Jerusalem among its people.

questions: What changes in our worship when we remember that God is not only good, but also sovereign over all creation and history?
Which modern idols more easily replace trust in the Lord, even without having a form of religious image?
How can our community respond in a concrete way to the repeated call to bless the Lord?
study.practice: Set up time for worship that will a memory and gratitude: remember a concrete action of God in your life, recognize your sovereignty over creation and your personal history, and transform it into prayer and praise. Then identify a false support in which you usually trust control, money, approval, or power - and abandon that trust, reaffirming your dependence on the living God. It is also worth practicing praise in community, not only privately, sharing with awareness of worship and encouraging others to bless the Lord.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow us to identify general connections with other psalms and the history of Israel, but do not provide secure data for additional date details, authorship, or specific occasion. The interpretation of Adam Clarke in 21 is presented as a restoration of the temple and the city, but this should be read as interpretative reading, not as a direct statement of the verse. There is also no basis for notes to detail more geography or chronology beyond what the text itself mentions.
